## Empirical Summary {#sec-empirical-summary}

The three experiments reveal a consistent pattern: **DGPs outperform single-layer GPs only when the target function has genuinely non-stationary, compositional structure**.

On the Kin8nm robot kinematics benchmark, DSVGP-2L achieved a 10.7% RMSE reduction over SVGP (0.0699 vs 0.0783) at full scale — the only dataset where deeper architectures provided a clear performance advantage. The target is a composition of trigonometric functions, precisely the hierarchical non-linearity where intermediate representations add value. On the two financial classification tasks, where credit-default surfaces are likely more smooth and monotonic, DGPs matched but did not meaningfully exceed single-layer GP performance (ROC-AUC within 0.002–0.004), confirming that a single RBF kernel is sufficient for this task.

Across all three datasets, the GP family delivered substantially better probability calibration than classical baselines. On the credit card dataset (22.1% default rate), GP models achieved 5–13$\times$ lower ECE than XGBoost. On the mortgage dataset (1.73% default rate), the calibration advantage amplified to 100$\times$ (ECE = 0.002–0.004 vs 0.400), confirming that Bayesian uncertainty quantification becomes proportionally more valuable at low base rates — a finding of direct importance for Basel IRB compliance where PD estimates must track observed frequencies.

The scaling analysis yields two practical guidelines. First, SVGP is the most data-efficient GP variant: it leads or matches DGPs at small scale ($N < 1{,}000$) across all experiments. Second, additional depth beyond two layers consistently degrades performance — DSVGP-3L collapsed to near-constant predictions at small scale (R² = 0.002 on Kin8nm, ROC-AUC = 0.510 on Freddie Mac) and never outperformed DSVGP-2L at any scale, while costing 3–4$\times$ more training time.

For practitioners, the implication is that DGPs warrant consideration when the application domain exhibits known compositional structure (robotics, sensor fusion, multi-stage physical processes) and sufficient data is available ($N > 3{,}000$). For smooth risk surfaces typical of credit and financial modelling, single-layer SVGPs provide comparable discriminative power at lower computational cost and with the same calibration benefits.
